utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Mr. Ivetic, I raised yesterday with Mr. Lukic the question of the additional information about the PJP commanders that the Prosecution seek, and he said that he would check during the day what the position was. Can you assist further on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have provided to the Office of the Prosecution the information that we have, that is the exact names of the persons and the exact units that they were involved in. We do not have the additional information that the Prosecution's office has sought. We have sought that information from the Serbian authorities, but obviously they have a lot more on their hands in recent days than our various requests. But we will reiterate them -- to them and ask for the information to be sent as soon as possible, and again we will advise the Prosecution accordingly. But we have provided the exact names of the individuals and the exact particular units that they were involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you what may sound a naive question, but why don't you ask your witnesses for the names of their fathers and their dates of birth and give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would, Your Honour, if we had been in contact with these persons. We just got this information from the Serbian authorities. We have not been in contact with all of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do they not have telephones or means of contact?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Some of the telephones are out of date that are on the information given from the Serbian authorities, Your Honour, but obviously where that's possible we would use that means to give the information and obviously if I had that information I would have no reason to not give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you have given names for witnesses, is that all you've told the Prosecution, the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the specific unit that they were involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we've given to the Office of the Prosecution, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And tell me, how many of these witnesses are you able to make contact with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One commander of a "ceta" that's it, out of the group that was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at least that one you can presumably get the information and give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'd also like you to do is let the Chamber have such communications as have taken place on this with the Government of Serbia so that we can see what we can do to assist and expedite this. We find it very difficult to understand why simple matters like this take so long to resolve, and we'd like to become involved ourselves in assisting with the difficulty -- to resolve the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the course of today, please, would you let Mr. Dawson have copies of all that's passed between you and the government so that we can see how we or consider how we might assist in this matter. Good afternoon, Mr. Lekoski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Zorko will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply throughout your evidence. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lekoski.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about you crossing the state border on the 27th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown again 6D1496, page 12 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, that's my passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you identify the two stamps on the document, one bears the inscription Donje Blace and the other one Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: If I'm right, you crossed the state border on 14th of April, 1999, going into Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Serbia, through the border post Donje Blace-Djeneral Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Typically I would cross the border on foot. I would first like to explain to the Trial Chamber why I went to Kosovo frequently. I have mentioned to you already that I had a sister in Blace. During the bombing, she was very ill and she also had a broken leg. So I was quite concerned for her, and I had to visit her frequently in order to take medication and other supplies that she needed. Given that she lived on meager means, her pension was 50 to 60 euros a month only, I also had to help her financially. And that was the main reason for me going into Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's quite enough as an answer to this question. You said that you crossed the border crossing on foot. Did you notice something unusual as you were crossing the border?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the border crossing at the Donje Blace, which is in the Republic of Macedonia, I saw a number of journalist crews, both local ones and foreign ones. Some of the foreign ones were CNN and BBC. I don't remember who the others were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you mentioned here crews of journalists. Did you see them on the Macedonian side of the border or on the Yugoslav side?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the Donje Blace border crossing, which is to say on the Macedonian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: That's the Macedonian side of the border I assume?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When you crossed the border and you stepped on the Yugoslav soil, did you notice something? Did you notice some civilians there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I crossed the border on foot and reached Djeneral Jankovic, which is on the Yugoslav side of the border, as soon as I passed through the passport control I noticed some 150 to 200 persons waiting to cross the border, the Djeneral Jankovic crossing, to enter Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Did you approach those civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that I had previously made arrangements with a friend from Pristina to take me to Pristina in a car and given that I had called him on the phone and he told me that he would reach the border crossing in 10 to 15 minutes, I simply stood there waiting for him to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. These civilians, can you describe whether among them or on them you could see some bruises or torn clothing or anything that would indicate some mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw nothing of the sort. I just saw that they had some bags they were carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned civilians. Did you see any members of the police or the army present there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw about ten policemen and several members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Would you be able to tell us what these policemen and members of the army did based on your recollection. Did they have any contact with civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were talking. The police stood in front of them and they had an ongoing dialogue about why they wanted to cross the border and go into Macedonia, or rather, why they were fleeing Kosovo. At that time the police were saying to them, You shouldn't flee, you should stay in your own homes, we can guarantee your safety, nothing would happen to you, go back to your homes. That was the gist of what they were saying to them. Civilians were not willing to accept that immediately, and they persisted in wanting to cross the border. And then the police asked them, Well, why do you want to flee? Nobody is chasing you away. We are offering you protection. Those who were talking to the police were saying that they had to leave Kosovo because that were the orders of the KLA, that's what the KLA had ordered them. Some of them mentioned that some ten days before the bombing started, the bombing of Yugoslavia, members of the verification mission came to their villages saying them that they needed to leave the country because the country would be bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. These civilians who engaged in the conversation with the policemen, did they eventually cross the border or did they go back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before that some officers -- I guess they were officers, I couldn't really tell what rank they were, officers of the Army of Yugoslavia approached them and joined the conversation. One of the officers said the same thing to them as the policemen did. He said, You should go back to your homes, you shouldn't flee, we shall guarantee your safety. If necessary, we will send guards to protect you in your villages, and they even offered escort that would take them to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Perhaps this will be a repetitive question, did they eventually cross the border or did they go back to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I stood there, they did not cross the border. They turned as if they wanted to go back. Now, as to whether they did go back, I don't know, because at that point in time my friend from Pristina arrived. I got into his car and continued on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. After crossing the border on this occasion, when did you go back to Macedonia from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was in the afternoon. I can't remember exactly, but I think it was between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, why was it you went to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I travelled to Pristina with my friend, who drove me to Pristina, and then from Pristina to Blace to visit my sister I travelled in a taxi; which means that my friend just drove me to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is Blace not on the way to Pristina from the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Blace comes after Pristina. So you need to pass through Podujevo and then another small town, I can't remember its name, and then comes Blace; and then from Blace you can continue on to Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a clarification. There is a town called Blace and there is a border crossing called Donje Blace. The border crossing is between Yugoslavia and Macedonia, and that's called Donje Blace; and as for the town of Blace it is a bit further away, and as far as I know it is not in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it surely is -- is it not somewhere near Stimlje, Blace?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not close to Pristina, Your Honours, it's a bit further away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, is it not near Stimlje is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not near Stimlje either. Most likely what's causing the confusion are the place names in Kosovo and Metohija which are similar or in some cases identical. We can see that, for example, there are several towns called Dubrava in Kosovo. Blace is located outside of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, on that occasion, as you were travelling back from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did you talk to members of police at the border crossing; and if so, what about?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was going back, as I reached the border crossing at Djeneral Jankovic, I asked a policeman about what had happened with the civilians. Did you manage to turn them back or did they go back or not? And he said to me that he knew that one group went back and that he didn't know about the rest of the group, and then also in passing he told me that on that same day a column of refugees had been bombed by NATO aviation, column travelling on the road from Prizren to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could I kindly ask you to speak a bit slower so that the interpreters can interpret everything accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 6D1496 again, page 8 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Do you see the document, Mr. Lekoski?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Do you see the stamp with inscription Donje Blace?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 26th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: If I'm right, you crossed the same border crossing on the 26th of May again?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: As you crossed the border on this occasion, did you notice something peculiar?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything on the Macedonian side of the border, nothing unusual; and then I crossed the border on foot and as I was approaching Djeneral Jankovic somewhere midway on the no man's land between the two borders, as I was some 40 to 50 metres away, I saw a group of people engaged in a passionate argument. And as I approached them I was able to discern what they were saying. I saw two or three young men standing there, and one of them said to civilians who were in front of them in Albanian: "bjere pasorshim," which in translation means: Give me your passports. When the civilian gave his passport to the man standing in front, he tore the passport immediately and then gave it back to him. The man whose passport had been torn immediately reacted and he said in Albanian: "pse e shkyn pasorshim," which in translation means: Why are you tearing my passport. The young man who had torn his passport reacted and said: "mos fol, ose te vras," which in translation means: Shut up or I'll kill you. He took his pistol out, he pointed it at him, and then he said in Albanian: "do folish policia e Maqedonise, pasoshin e ka shkye policia serbe," which in translation means: You'll tell the Macedonian policemen that your passport had been torn by the Serbian police, that's what I saw in passing and I passed by them and went on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lekoski. During 1999, given that you told us that you live in Gostivar in Macedonia, during that year did you have occasion to talk to people who had fled the area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have occasion. Gostivar is a town that is mostly populated by Albanians, they are the majority population, and in the vicinity of Gostivar there were two refugees camps. One camp was set up in the village of Cegrane and one could see it with the naked eye travelling from Gostivar towards Tetovo, it was on the right-hand side. It was set up in the foot of the Suva Gora mountain so that one could see it from a distance, one could see white tents. The other camp was set up in the village of Gradac, on the other side of the highway, and it wasn't visible. The refugees arrived in thousands on a daily basis. They came to Gostivar to buy the supplies that they needed in their camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lekoski. Did you manage to talk to any of the people from the camps or to talk to somebody in Gostivar?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion. I can't remember the exact date, but I know that sometime in May, I know it was a Saturday, since I didn't go to work to Skopje on that day, I just went to town to buy something for my house. I went to the market where they were selling vegetables, greengrocers market. At the time it was in the centre of the town, and as I approached a stand I could hear the conversation between the buyer and the seller there. The buyer said that he was a refugee from Kosovo and that he lived in the camp in Cegrane. He was complaining about the accommodation, the food, saying that a lot of them there were ill, that they regretted the fact that they had fled Kosovo due to conditions in the camps, and he said that they were not faring well in Macedonia at all. And when he mentioned Macedonia I joined in the conversation and then I asked him, Why did you then flee to Macedonia? He said that he had been ordered to do that by the KLA. If they had not fled, they would have been killed. After that I asked him, Did you have some other problems? Did somebody else persecute you? And he said, No, I had normal contacts both with the police and the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lekoski, was that the only conversation you had from any refugee from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had another conversation, I think it was in late May or early June, I don't quite remember. I went to the hospital, since my brother worked there and continues to work there as a doorman, and I went to talk to him on that occasion. I asked those people there, Where's my brother? And they said to me that he was around but had gone to run an errand. So I stood in front of the hospital waiting for him, and a person was standing next to me, I guess waiting to have an examination or something like that. He and I started talking informally. I asked him where he was from. He said that he was a refugee from Kosovo. And then I asked him, Well, what are you waiting for here? And he said, Well, I'm waiting to see a doctor because I'm sick. I continued talking to him and I asked him, Well, why did you flee to Macedonia? And he said that he had fled due to NATO bombing solely and that he was afraid of the war. As I continued talking to him, I asked him whether he had any other problems, and he said, No, I am from Kacanik and I frequently cross the border between Serbia and Macedonia, and I never had any problems, either with police or with the army. He even told me that one month prior to that the verification mission people came to see them and that they were trying to convince them to leave Kosovo. And since they were close to the border they told them to go to Macedonia, saying that they would only be in transit in Macedonia, and that from there they would be taken to Western countries. The person I talked to, I remember this well, is called Kuma Hamid, he was from Kacanik and he was living in a private accommodation in a village called Forino, the village of Forino is not far from Gostivar, some 7 to 8 kilometres. It is practically right next to the village of Cegrane, where the refugee camp was. The man where he lived was either a friend of his or a relative, I didn't ask him. I waited there for a few more minutes, and since my brother didn't come and I was in a hurry to go to work I went away from the hospital and continued on running my errands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lekoski. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zorko. No other Defence examination? Mr. Lekoski, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, are you or were you in 1999 the coordinator of a group called the Association of Clubs of Serbs and Montenegrins and Macedonians in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that club aligned to any political movement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a purely civic association, non-political, totally non-political.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, when you say "civic," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a club. It was associations that primarily dealt in humanitarian affairs, cultural affairs, bringing people together, that's what those associations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, as the leader or coordinator of that club, did you have occasion in 1999 to visit Kosovo, Pristina in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I beg your pardon. During 1999, no; but before that, I did pay visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times did you visit Kosovo before 1999 in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many times I visited, but when I would visit it would only be for humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, did you not visit Kosovo and Metohija in your capacity of leader of this group at all in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As leader of that group, did you not hold a press conference in Pristina on the 11th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to focus on my questions now because I didn't ask you anything about bombing as yet. I've asked you more than once about 1999. Is your answer yes, you -- as leader of the group you conducted a press conference where members of the press attended in Pristina in February, the 11th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that you had asked me whether I was there as that kind of a leader during the bombing. As for what you're asking now, yes, that is correct, I did have a press conference at the Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times in 1999 did you go to Pristina in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember how many times I went there. I went perhaps about 20 times to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but that was primarily because of my professional work, because I worked and I was head of a firm from Yugoslavia, that was Toza Markovic, that was the company, so I travelled on official business and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm so sorry. I'm just asking you how many times in 1999 that you went to Kosovo and Metohija in the capacity as head of the group. You have told us about the third occasion in February. I'm just asking how many times.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I told you. I went, say, 20 times or 30 times that year, in 1999, to Serbia. And as for what I testified about until now, that is that I visited my sister three times, that is correct; but how many times I was there -- well, if you have specific information remind me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, you're only being asked how often you went to Kosovo, Kosovo, in your capacity as the head of the association, the coordinator of the association in the year 1999. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I've already said. Once when I held that press conference at the Grand Hotel, and I don't remember about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who attended with you at that press conference in 1999, the 11th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there was this one man with me from Kumanovo, his name was Marijan Miteski.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was his -- who was he?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there not also a Miroljub Zaric who also attended with you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a Tanjug journalist from Skoplje, at that time he was Tanjug correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he not also a leader of a political party or a group?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps he was a member of some party. He did not head a party, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you issue a statement that was published in Tanjug in which you expressed full support to the leadership of Serbia and FRY in their efforts to resolve the Kosovo crisis?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible that you might have done so and not recall? Don't you -- well, let me ask you this: Don't you recall that your attendance at this press conference was reported in the press?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object on the grounds of relevance. This -- we've had I think several witnesses talk about Rambouillet and how everyone in the international community was hoping to resolve the crisis in Kosovo. So I don't see what this has to do with the witness's testimony or with what is relevant for these proceedings, apart from trying to badger the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For all the reasons Mr. Ivetic gives, this is very relevant evidence. Please continue with the questioning, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The purpose of your attending a press conference in Pristina was for the press to publish what you had to say. Weren't you aware that what you said was reported in the press, including Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the records, Your Honours, we have not been provided any documentation by the Office of the Prosecution that they intend to use for cross-examination with this witness that bears on this topic. If Mr. Stamp has a document, I believe he's trying to go by the back door around the rules that we have established in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not tendered a document or attempted to use a document with the witness just now, and in addition to that if I were to use a document, the document is an open-source document, the document is a -- read in newspaper reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't have to intimate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would have to, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed with the question. Let's see where you get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Weren't you aware, for the third time, Mr. -- sir, that your statements in Pristina on the 11th of February were reported in the press?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that because journalists were there and it went without saying that that would be made public, but I have to tell you that it was Marijan Miteski who talked most of the time at that press conference. So I state with full responsibility that I don't really remember what it was that I said then. If I did say something, could you please present it to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you not say that you give full support to the leaderships of Serbia and the FRY in their efforts to resolve the Kosovo crisis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, if he's relying on a document or not, I would like to know the foundation for this question. I think I'm entitled, especially since we asked the Office of the Prosecution for any and all statements they claim came from any of our witnesses, and thus far I believe that we received nothing for this witness. If this is another situation where they say they have nothing and then all of a sudden they have something later on, I believe this is an issue of fair play that must be addressed. I apologise for having to stand on this issue, but counsel says he no document, but all his questions indicate he does have a document. So what are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're talking about an oral statement that it is alleged the witness made and that is what the question is about. So please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, I do not remember. I've already told you that I don't remember. Please present to me what it was that I had said because it's been nine years since then, and we cannot really remember everything that we said, can we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, you've given us a very clear recollection of a number of events in 1999, you've even quoted what people were saying on these occasions in 1999. Now you say you can't remember what you said yourself. That's what counsel is asking you about, what you actually said. Would you do your best to try to remember, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to address you and say the following. In addition to my professional responsibilities and the life I've had in Macedonia, at this point in time I am a lay judge at my court in Gostivar. At the proposal of the court in Gostivar, I was an officially elected person by the parliament of Macedonia. What I'm saying here is the truth. What I experienced, what I saw, not more, not less. I wish to assure you, Your Honours, you can check this, you can check what kind of a lay judge I am at my court in Gostivar, and if you find a single judgement that I signed and that was not on the side of the truth, I am prepared to be held accountable here before you in terms of criminal liability, moral liability, material liability, whatever you wish. Throughout my life, I have pursued the truth and suffered for the truth, and that is the case until this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, you were asked a question and we would like you to try to answer the question. We can only judge your credibility as a witness once we've heard everything that has to be said. So will you please address the question of whether you can remember saying what Mr. Stamp has quoted to you in the context of the extremely important tense international situation surrounding Rambouillet around the 11th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert before you with full responsibility that I do not recall what it was that I had said. If I am shown what it was, perhaps I may remember; but I state with full responsibility that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall if any member of your party at that press conference made that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe somebody did say something, and if somebody did say something it must have been the president of the party, Marijan Miteski from Kumanovo, because he was the one who was really in charge of the press conference, he did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's look at it from a different point of view. What was the purpose of the press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do not remember exactly now why this press conference had been called, but it was probably in order to express what the Prosecutor said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You seriously -- do you often give press conferences? Perhaps I'm misunderstanding the situation. You often give press conferences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that time we just happened to be together in Pristina. I was there as coordinator of these associations in order to discuss humanitarian matters. Since at that point in time the president of that party was there, we went out together at this press conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you telling us on full responsibility that you don't remember the purpose of the press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not say that. I said that a press conference had been called, as the Prosecutor claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, you seem to be saying now that you were in Pristina for some business and you were just invited to a press conference that you attended, but you told us earlier just a few minutes ago, and this is at line 22 of page 15 of the transcript: "Yes, yes, I've already said. Once when I held that press conference at the Grand Hotel, and I don't remember the rest."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, we've just received a copy from the Prosecution of the document they claim they're not using -- they don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not clear to me at the moment, Mr. Ivetic, that a document is being used. There are two separate matters that could arise: One relates to the conduct of the cross-examination and so far no document has been referred to; the other, however, is one of disclosure. Are you saying this was not disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would not be up on my feet if it had been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At any stage? It has never been disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is my understanding it has not. We specifically asked for all of our witnesses, any documents the Prosecution had in their possession, particularly anything they claimed to be statements, and we received a negative response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is that we are not obliged to disclose to the Defence matters -- well, when I say "disclose," I mean directly disclose to the Defence, documents which do not fall under Rule 68 or Rule 66, when the document -- especially documents which are on -- which are open-source documents which can be located by the Defence by searching either the electronic database, which we give them access to, or by doing web searches themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just make a comment regarding what it was that the Prosecutor just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document cannot be found when searching the internet using the name of this witness, and I hear from my colleagues now that the document doesn't seem to show up on EDS either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me on that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I would need to check actually to see if documents which are part of the -- which are open-source documents which we can search and find are not on the EDS. My information, and I will be prepared to be corrected, is that these documents are on the EDS. Secondly, I cannot understand why it is that the name of the witness would not appear on the document, on the EDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, every document in EDS has an ERN number. This document that was just disclosed to us does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What Mr. Visnjic is saying that by putting the witness's name into a search engine this document is not disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the document would not be located -- as I said, I will check that, whether or not it could be searched. This document is a translation, I believe, of -- of a Tanjug report, and my understanding is that this document appears on the EDS system. But I would have to check that. If Mr. Ivetic says it can't be found, I can't say that just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In any event, what do you intend to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do not intend at this stage, since the document was not disclosed to the Defence, to use it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the document is a foundation I can use to ask this witness [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think when we broke off, Witness, you were saying that the reason why you don't remember what the press conference was about was because you were in Pristina for some other business and simply invited to a press conference. And I'd like to remind you that you said earlier today in your testimony that you held a conference, a press conference. So I ask again, did you hold that press conference in your capacity as leader or member of this group? Or is your earlier testimony not true?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to this principle that we have in Macedonia, press conferences are predominantly held by political parties. I said from the very outset that this association, whose coordinator I was, had just one task, and that is for -- I mean, these are non-political, non-party organizations. And it was humanitarian and cultural work that they focused on, and that is the only reason why I was there. And then this party leader happened to be there, we happened to meet in Pristina, and that's how I came to this press conference. I don't remember that I said anything at this press conference. If I did say something, could you please present it to me so that I remember because, indeed, it has been nine years since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember while you were in Pristina on that occasion meeting Zoran Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not meet Zoran Andjelkovic. I met with the Red Cross on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you ever met Zoran Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely for that purpose, we were talking about humanitarian work. Because at the time, not only before did I bring in the help that was needed, but before then I sent a lot of humanitarian help from Macedonia. And besides that I made my personal contribution in humanitarian aid when the Muslims from Bosnia were located at Mavrovo in 1993 in the village of Bunec. Then I made my own personal contribution. Also when the tsunami happened in Indonesia. I was a humanitarian worker in general. I donated blood over 25 times in my own country and my work in that organization was actually based exclusively on humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when this CNN or this person, a party from CNN with the mike, assaulted this lady on the 27th of March you said, was -- weren't there numerous newspaper and press -- well, media persons on the Albanian side of the border at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the Albanian side of the border. It's a mistake, the Albanian -- or on the Albanian side of the border. Are you thinking of the Macedonian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you going -- I'm sorry. Sorry, the Macedonian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was passing through the border, there was only one camera placed in the middle of the road, and that was a CNN camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Nothing further from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask for a short break before we start our re-examination in order to be able to consult with my colleagues. The situation is a little unusual. The source of the document is unknown, and my learned friend quoted some things from the document but not completely. So I would just like to be allowed to have a brief pause before continuing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long is it you're asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 minutes, Your Honours, would be quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we'll do is take 20 minutes, resume at quarter to 4.00, and then re-arrange the length of the other two sessions for the afternoon to ensure that we still sit for the same length of time. And meanwhile, you can take whatever steps you require to take to investigate the matter you wish to check. Mr. Lekoski, counsel wishes time to consider the position before deciding on re-examination and what to ask you. While that happens, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. Please remain in the room to which you're taken, and we will see you again at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since my learned friend drew his questions from material that was not disclosed to us earlier, we believe that it would be in the interests of justice to show the document to the witness on the ELMO so that we could see what is written in the document and to put questions to him about the exact spoken words at this press conference, with your permission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lekoski, can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you please look at the third paragraph, and I'm going to read to you what it says and the interpreters will translate what is written here. [In English] "'We give full support to the leaderships of Serbia and FRY in their efforts to resolve the Kosovo and Metohija crisis peacefully and through a political dialogue, and we are opposed to any blackmail and military threats to Yugoslavia.' Lekoski said and stressed that the problems in the Balkans should be resolved by the nations of the Balkans, who knows each other best." [Interpretation] Mr. Lekoski, several questions were put to you. I would just like to put this to you. Do you stand by the words you stated here and do you recall stating this at that press conference?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, having seen the document, yes, this is what I said on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this document for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that we have this, perhaps we should look more closely at it, since this is the first time the Trial Chamber has seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to ask more questions from the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let us just keep it there for a moment. Mr. Lekoski, was the Socialist Christian Party a Macedonian party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was a Macedonian party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your link with President Gligorov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have any connections with President Gligorov, but if you insist I did have one encounter or meeting with President Gligorov, this was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This report starts by saying: "Macedonia and its president, Kiro Gligorov, whose views we are conveying, absolutely favour a peaceful solution for the Kosovo and Metohija crisis. Zivko Lekoski ... stated in Pristina today." So the report says that you're speaking for the president. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I was not in a position to speak on behalf of the president because I was not a member of parliament or of the government or anything to do with the president. Before that we had one meeting with President Gligorov where we asked him to -- or for Macedonia to be neutral as far as the arrival of NATO troops was concerned because they were passing through Macedonia. On that occasion we also urged that this be done in a peaceful, principled manner, which President Gligorov also confirmed that that's what he was also committed to. So the main commitment of the association that I headed was economic, cultural, and overall civilizational links among the countries of the Balkans and broader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly, but I think that it was a few days or maybe ten days before the bombing. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember all that well who was there, but the people who were mentioned here were definitely not present. I know that -- just let me remember a little bit. One of my deputies of the association was there, his name was Slobodan, but I cannot remember his last name, Slobodan Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that meeting before the press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you suggest then any basis on which Tanjug may have reported that you were conveying views of the president of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know why this was done. First of all, I could not be conveying the positions or the views of the president. I was not an important player in any of that and I didn't have any authority to convey anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us now that you've seen this who organized the press conference and how you came to be involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who organized the press conference. I was in Pristina at the time, at the Red Cross; and after that we went together to the conference. I think the conference was organized at the Pristina Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say you went together to the press conference, together with whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the people I see here, Miteski and Miroljub Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did they also meet with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, they were not with me. I was by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How then did you come to meet up with them and go to the press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We came together to Pristina from Macedonia, and then I went on my way and they went on their way; after that we met up. We went back together, too, in one vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you give this a number, Mr. Haider?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that will be IC 189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should also upload this in e-court and give it an appropriate number when you do that. Mr. Zorko, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what we will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, I'm just going to have a couple more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: You said that you lived in Gostivar?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Predominantly inhabited by the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if you have and how many friends do you have among members of the Albanian community?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, my first next-door neighbours are Albanians, they live next door to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My objection is that this doesn't arise from the cross-examination. Mr. Zorko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say in response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that the questions of my learned friend were also something that created doubts about the credibility of the witness in a kind of indirect, round-about way. Since the information from this document was used only partially, so I'm only putting questions that can point to the weight one can attribute to the testimony of this witness, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The particular question you've asked, which I don't think has anything to do with the document, does seem to us to arise from the line of cross-examination that was pursued, and we will allow you to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lekoski, I'm going to repeat my question. Do you have, and if you do, how many friends do you have among the Albanian ethnic community in the community where you live?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing that I have to say is that my next-door neighbours are Albanians and we have excellent relations, we visit one another every day. That is the first thing. Secondly, I have many in town that I see every day. We have coffee, we talk, and so on and so forth. And thirdly, when I was working in the company in Skoplje, my best buyers and the most honest buyers were Albanians. None of the Albanian companies owed anything to my company. The Macedonians were left owing my company something, but not the Albanians. So I have excellent cooperation with them, and we lived very well together then and we still do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one more question. Since after my examination-in-chief you also said that you were a lay judge, are you aware of the gravity and the seriousness of your testimony before this Tribunal and the consequences of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO LEKOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZORKO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zorko. Mr. Lekoski, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to assist us. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we proceed, can I say something. Since I said something in respect to the document before, I have consulted about the circumstances and the document on a search of the EDS, the electronic disclosure system, would not be available, but the document is an open-source document that could have been discovered by the Defence with a diligent search of the internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if you've done another diligent search just to confirm that, but Mr. Visnjic's point was that he tried and failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if he -- a diligent search includes a variation of spellings of the names in Cyrillic, in the way Tanjug is published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect he's conscious of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. That is what I have been advised. I have not done so myself. Secondly, the Prosecution maintains that the results of these open-source searches, unless they fall under the Rules, Rule 68 in particular at this stage of the case, are not disclosable; under the Rules, we are not obliged to disclose them. However, seeing how it can cost some time we will consider just handing them over if we find anything on the net with the name of a witness on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful to hear you say that, but there's a separate issue which is one related to the actual use of the document in cross-examination which has to be intimated. Now, Mr. Ivetic is identifying a fault-line in the definition of use of the document for cross-examination, and therefore it's necessary for you to give careful thought to whether albeit you don't actually put the document in front of the witness, you're effectively using it in such a way that fairness demands that a copy is or that intimation's given that this would be the source of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not an order that you do it; it's an order to be cautious in considering which documents do, in fact, require to be disclosed in terms of our rule about requiring disclosure of documents being used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Can I just say this, it had been intended to be disclose that one along with another one a few days ago and by some oversight it was not, and therefore we thought it could be used as a -- well, as a foundation, a good-faith foundation to ask questions, but not to impeach. So its use would have been limited in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Ivetic, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next witness would be Nebojsa Ognjenovic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope Mr. Stamp saying that there was another one that was not disclosed to me, and I hope this won't come back to bite me with the next witness. If there's any another document not disclosed then, assuming he means with respect to the witnesses already past, but we'll deal with that if it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the re-arranged schedule would require a break at 5.15 for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Ognjenovic. For purposes of the record, can you please introduce yourself giving your full name.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Good day. My name is Nebojsa Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly about yourself and your educational background.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Prizren, where I completed elementary school and secondary school as well as a post-secondary teacher's college in Prizren. Now I live in Belgrade as a temporarily displaced person from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you please now tell us about your employment history within the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I started working in the Ministry of Internal Affairs in 1982, and I was assigned to the traffic police station in Kosovska Mitrovica up until 1983. In 1983 I was assigned to the Vrbnica police station for the control of border crossings, that is near Prizren. All the way up until 1999, when we withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija, I worked there; and then from 1999 until 2003 I worked at Belgrade airport at the police station at the border crossing there, so that was until 2003. Until the 30th of June, 2006, I worked at the department of the border police in the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade. Since that date, the 30th of June, 2006, I've been a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And can you tell us what your specific work assignment was in the time-period 1998 and 1999 and what specific duties that position entailed.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: As for the police station for border crossings, in 1998 and in 1999, I worked there as the commander, "komandir," of the station. My tasks involved planning and exercising control over the work of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the police station at the Vrbnica border crossing, such as where the scene is located and how large of an area the border crossing comprises.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The building itself of the Vrbnica station is 17 kilometres away from Prizren on the road going to Tirana. The building is a proper house, solid, consisting of 25 rooms. We used only four rooms because of the scope of our work. Four were used by the police and four by the customs officials who were there at the border crossing. The area of the border crossing, according to the agreement, included 50 metres to the left and right of the middle lane of the road at the Albanian border crossing and 200 metres from the borderline that is on the bridge between the two border crossings into our territory. That was the area of the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can you explain for us the difference between the border crossing and the border belt area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The border crossing is a place that is designated for crossing the state border, for persons who meet the requirements set by law in order to cross the state border. Staying and moving at the border crossing is under the control of the police that works at the border crossing police station. The border belt area, however, is the area from the borderline itself into the territory of the country itself. That was 100 metres, but sometime in the 1990s this border belt was expanded and it became 10 kilometres long. The villages that are along this area were not duty-bound to have special permits for moving about in the area. Movement in the border area was checked by the members of the Army of Yugoslavia or, to put it more precisely, the guards from the border post at that border crossing. It was the Veljko Vlahovic border post in my specific case. And there was only a metal fence between us. This means that -- this means that if a person has a permit to move about and stay there and wishes to do so, that person will be checked by the members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Could you or any of the policemen at the Vrbnica station move out with the border crossing into the border belt area on your own?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: We could not go on our own. If we needed to go, we would have to report to the closest border post, or rather, the Vrbnica border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could please tell us, who controlled the transport of goods at the border crossing and how was this regulated?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The control of traffic of goods was carried out by the customs officials at this border crossing in accordance with the laws regulating customs, so they were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us to what governmental structure or organ this customs service was subordinated; that is to say, was it a part of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. The customs service did not belong to the Ministry of the Interior. The customs service belonged and does belong to the Ministry of Finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is the Ministry of Finance a republican level or a -- or was it a federal level ministry at the time, in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was at federal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, focusing on the -- on your station, the police station, at the Vrbnica border crossing, which organizational structure within the Ministry of Internal Affairs did your station belong to and how was the line of work within that structure set up?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The border police station belonged to the administration of the border police, whose headquarters were in Belgrade. We were directly under them, or rather, they were our direct superiors. According to the structure of jobs, there was the commander, the deputy commander, the assistant commander of the police station, then four shift leaders, and 17 policemen. That was the job structure for the station that I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to the station where you were at how police officers would be -- what their appearance would be, what they would wear in the course of their duties?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The members of this station had regular uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how many other similar police stations fell directly under the subordination of the headquarters -- the administration of the border police whose headquarters were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The administration of the border police in the ministry has 38 stations within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the course of your work at the border police station of Vrbnica, what regulations did you utilise?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: At border police stations, all the laws applied in the Ministry of the Interior were applied there too. Due to the subject matter that we dealt with, we mostly relied on the law on border crossings and on staying and moving about in the border area, then the law on passports of Yugoslavia and the law on the movement of foreign persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What were the specific daily tasks undertaken by employees of your station at the Vrbnica border crossing?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The primary task of the employees was to enable unhindered crossing of the border by persons who wished to cross the state border with proper documents, passports; then to provide security for the building and the area of the border crossing too. Those were the primary tasks of the employees of this station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what basic documentation was necessary under the law existing in 1999 to permit a person to cross the state border?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The only relevant document for crossing the state border is a passport, a passport, that document. There are several types of passports. If necessary, I can mention all of them. Children's passports, joint passports, diplomatic passports, service passports, then also there is the institution of the lesse passe. A lesse passe is issued to persons who lost their passport in a foreign country. Diplomatic and service passports are issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to these passports, in order to leave the -- in order to legally leave the country, would the passport have to then at that point in time be valid and in force?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, if the person wishes to leave the country, the passport has to be a valid one. If the passport is not valid, the person will not be allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Under what circumstances would FRY citizens be denied exit across the state border?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: FRY citizens would be denied exit across the state border if they do not possess a valid passport or if the passport was damaged, is technically deficient. That means that if it was damaged or if there is no room left for affixing a seal. Then that person will be sent back to correct this passport at the organ that issued the passport in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it possible under the law to cross the state border outside the border crossing and without the paperwork foreseen for such a crossing; and if so, under what specific circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The border could be crossed only at specified border crossings. Exceptionally, the border can be crossed without documents if there is a natural disaster involved. This means a flood, an earthquake, war operations, that is to say that it was only in those situations that a person would be allowed to cross the state border without creating a border incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what article of the then-current law on crossing the state border would have been applicable to such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was Article 8, Article 8 of the law on crossing the state border and movement in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could focus for a moment to the time-period before the start of the war with the NATO forces. We have heard here in this court of plans for defence brought at the level of the RJB including measures in case of an aggression against the FRY. Did you receive any documentation relating to any such matters?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have Exhibit 6D269 up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would ask you if, first of all, you could look at the title of this document and then the list of recipients that says SPP -- oh, I see the English does have the translation, but could you confirm for us what the acronym SPP stands for.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: This acronym stands for: To the border police stations, all of them, from 1 to 35, to the commanders, "komandir," of these stations, which is to say that this dispatch was sent to all border police stations. It was a circular letter. This means that we were an independent station. As you can see in the heading, all SUPs received it, the MUP staff in Pristina, we as an independent station, and underneath RDB just for their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, do you recognise this document as being the one that you received regarding any defence plans brought at the level of the RJB?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In case there was an aggression against SFRY, or rather, FRY by NATO and underneath it lists the measures that all above-listed entities need to undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said a little time ago, Mr. Ognjenovic, that there were 38 border police stations. This says 1 to 35. It may not matter, but what is the correct number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time there were 35. I gave the new figure because after that two stations were added, the one at the Belgrade airport and the one at the harbour in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at page 2, paragraphs 6 and 8 of this document, sir, this should be the same in both the English and the Serbian. I would ask you do these paragraphs spell out the concrete measures for stations such as yours in the event of aggression and could you explain them for the members of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Item 6 and item 8 pertain to stations. So this is a mandatory dispatch. We had to abide by it and undertake measures listed in this dispatch, which is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the information of the Trial Chamber, was the border crossing at Vrbnica officially open to travellers prior to the start of the air war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: From the 21st of May, 1998, this post was closed for travellers. It was only open for crossing to our citizens who were abroad and also for foreigners who wanted to leave our territory. There were several cases where several Germans crossed the border going from Albania into our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take the time to delve into the work of the border police stations. With respect to the employees of the -- of the police station Vrbnica, who decides -- who decided on their assignment and scope of work at the station?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It was the administration for border police that decided on their assignment and I as their immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who would be empowered to decide on personnel changes, personnel promotions, commendations, or disciplinary actions for employees of the border police station?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It was the administration of border police in Belgrade that decided on appointments when it comes to police employees. When it comes to commanders, it was the chief of the public security sector who decided on appointments. My decision on my appointment was signed by Radovan Stojcic. Decisions for employees or concerning employees are issued at the proposal of the commander, "komandir," of a police station and with his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In 1998 -- in 1998 and in 1999, what role or impact could either the MUP staff in Pristina or the secretariat of interior in Prizren have with respect to the foregoing matter, that is to say the personnel changes, promotion, commendation, or disciplinary actions of employees of the border police station Vrbnica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Not only during this period of time but in general, nobody except for the border police administration could decide on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the national ethnic make-up during the 1990s at the Vrbnica border police station?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: In the 1990s, there were nine police employees working at the station, out of which six were Albanians, of Albanian ethnic minority, and three were Serbs. And then in late 1990s the Albanian workers left the ministry of their own free will, four of them did. So if necessary I can give you their names. Out of which two met the requirements for retirement. The remaining two Albanians stayed on working for some time; however, Ahmed Ramaj, under pressure from his son, who was irredenta was forced to leave the service. He left the service under sad circumstances. So that the ministry was forced to send in additional workers from other provinces of Serbia to help out with work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any disciplinary proceedings instituted against members of your border police station that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There were no disciplinary proceedings against members of this station or employees of this station except in two cases where policemen were fined financially due to light violations of their work duties. This was a 20 per cent reduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In those two cases, what were the circumstances of the light violations of their work duties and what can you tell us about the two employees?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding these two, a light or minor violation is, for example, disorderly appearance in terms of their uniforms, being late for work, and similar minor violations of work duties and obligations. When it comes to minor violations of work duties and obligations, a commander of the police station gives a proposal and the border police administration issues a decision on how they are to be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to these two, what was the final outcome of the decision or the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were fined in such a way that 20 per cent of their monthly salary was deducted, one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the border police station required to operate under or prepare any plans of work and reports relating to the same; and if so, to whom would these reports be sent?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Every station within the ministry drafted plans and submitted reports. Our particular station received forms from the administration, based on which we submitted reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you also receive any plan of work from any other structure within the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to whom would reports on these drafted plans be sent and why?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
