utterances.text: The plans and work reports were the following. There were daily reports, monthly, and annual work reports. Daily and monthly work reports were sent to the regional secretariat, to the RDB, and one copy remained at the station. As for annual reports, we sent them to the border police administration. I will correct myself. We also sent monthly reports to the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say the border police administration, again, where would that be located?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The border police administration is in the ministry seat in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this procedure remain the same and in place the entire time from when you were appointed in the early 1990s to the Vrbnica border station all the way up until June of 1999 when you withdrew?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: That's how it was before and that's how it is now, when it comes to reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How would you receive dispatches, or "depese," before and during the air war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: We received dispatches via the regional secretariat, which was the one in Prizren, the Prizren SUP, since we did not have technical resources to receive it ourselves at the border crossing. However, during NATO bombing the situation was difficult. So on a number of occasions, we had to send a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the Vrbnica border crossing and your station there within, what types of documentation were kept in the ordinary course of operations of that station?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the records? Is that what you have in mind, the records kept at the station?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: At the border crossing police stations, there are about 38 types of records, various books, forms, and so on. Books that we kept concerning the crossing of the state border were as follows. The book on the travel of passengers, book on visas that were issued, on issued tourist passes, on permits for movement and stay of foreigners -- I mean persons who came to the area of the border crossing, records kept on the entry of foreign damaged vehicles entering the country, and then other kinds of registry books that I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've already discussed reports relating to the monthly, daily, and yearly planned work of the border station. Did you also have occasion to report about any unusual activity at the police station; and if so, to whom would those reports be transmitted?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There were official notes made regarding every action of employees at the police stations, either notes or reports. These official notes or reports were sent by us to the border police administration in Belgrade, to the staff in Pristina, to the border police department in the relevant secretariat, which was the one in Prizren, the SUP in Prizren. And then depending on the issue involved, we would also send it either to the traffic police or to the crime investigation police depending on the subject matter of that particular official note.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 6D129 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a document I'd like to have your assistance with, sir. You'll see it's a dispatch dated the 1st of September, 1998, and the origin is the MUP Republic of Serbia UKP. Could you tell us whether the UKP was a structure that you fell under or reported to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The UKP is the criminal police administration. We didn't submit any reports to them, but since we're talking about aliens here who committed crimes and there is a possibility that they would leave the territory of our country, then all the border crossings in the -- on the territory of the republic were informed immediately as independent stations. So the SUPs and the border stations were each informed separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to any actions that you would undertake if said criminal perpetrators found themselves at the border, how would those actions or your steps be governed? That is to say, what would -- how would you -- based upon what would you act?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Each dispatch has a measure that should be adhered to. Here it says if the -- if you find something out in connection with the aforementioned, then you should notify the person. There's a number here. So if this person should turn up at the border crossing, such and such a person responsible for that would be informed and then they would tell us which measures would need to be taken in relation to these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to start focusing for a moment at 1999 and the time-period of the NATO bombings. Did you, sir, in the course of your work at the border police station at Vrbnica become aware of the existence of any plan on the part of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia to forcibly displace and/or deport members of the ethnic Albanian national minority from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never received that or saw anything like that, nor would I do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the border police station Vrbnica ever receive any written orders or oral instructions from your superiors within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia to take personal documentation and travel documents from persons of the ethnic Albanian national minority as they crossed the state border?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, we never received anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And a third, similar question. Did the border police station at the Vrbnica border crossing ever receive written or oral instructions from your superiors within the Serbian MUP to take car registration plates from persons of ethnic Albanian nationality leaving the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive a document like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say you didn't receive a document like that. Did you ever receive any oral orders to that effect?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, from the commencement of the NATO bombing onwards, was the border crossing at Vrbnica ever mined with explosives?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what knowledge or information you have with regards to that, what areas were mined, when, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There are two exit lanes while exiting the country. The left lane until the very bridge on the line of the border was mined and anti-tank barricades were placed there and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: And nothing else was mined in the border crossing area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there minefields on the road or the area leading to the border crossing Vrbnica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The Prizren border crossing road at the Zur intersection, until the very line of the border or the border crossing, some 6 kilometres of the left and the right side were mined off the lanes, next to the roadways.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how far is the crossing road at the Zur intersection from the very line of the border at the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how often would you travel that road during 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I went every day from my house in Prizren to the border crossing, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were there any control check-points located either in the border crossing area or the road leading to the border crossing area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: On the road, yes, but not at the border crossing itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were these control check-points operated by legitimate state authorities; and if so, whom?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The check-points were at the town exit where the Army of Yugoslavia was. The intersection at the Zur village was a joint check-point of the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the -- did the police have any role in placing the mines at the border crossing and the region leading up to the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. As the immediate superior, I did not know that the roads would be mined at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the war with NATO, that is, in 1999, how many policemen were employed at the Vrbnica border crossing station during each work shift and how many shifts were there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: According to the classification mentioned earlier, it was 100 per cent. We worked in 12-48/12-48 [as interpreted] shifts, meaning 12 hours of a day shift, 24 hours off; 12 hours night shift, 48 hours off. There could be four or five policemen at the most at the night shift.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was we worked 12-24/12-48 shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The -- with respect to the shift, the five -- four to five policemen on each shift, what would their duties be? Would each of the officers or policemen have the same duties or would they be somehow differentiated?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They could not have the same duties. Somebody had to be at the duty service, somebody had to secure the border crossing area, somebody had to check the passengers. So practically the number of employees was not sufficient, in view of the conditions that prevailed in that area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we recall that you identified that there was an area that was mined, did anyone secure that area so that civilians would not enter the mined area; and if so, whom?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the police officers did this from the border crossing. They directed the columns in such a way that no one would step on a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say that the police officers did this from the border crossing, are you talking about the same four to five police officers or policemen that would be on a given shift, a given time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they switched. It wasn't always the same person. They would switch. Sometimes I myself also did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was the first time that a group of citizens appeared at the Vrbnica border crossing intending to pass without the possession of valid travel documents?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: A group appeared on the 27th of March, 1999, at about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to this particular group that appeared on the 27th of March, 1999, can you tell us what ethnic nationality were these persons, how many of them there were, and what approximate age group they fell in?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: About 97 men, women, and children were there. They came to the border crossing area on tractors and some agricultural machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And insofar as they did not have valid paperwork or documentation, what steps did you take towards these individuals?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: We did not permit them to leave our country, but because they insisted persistently, we took some measures in order to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could tell indeed what measures you took to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I informed the border police administration at the seat of the ministry in Belgrade by telephone, and I explained what it was all about, after which I received an answer that I should try to dissuade the persons from going to Albania. But the persons persistently refused, only wanting to go to Albania and not to go back in any event. These were women and children that we're talking about, so I came to the border and I got in touch with the Albanian border authorities and I explained to them what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were these persons eventually permitted to leave the country, that is, to leave the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and enter into Albania; and if so, how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I had to get in touch with the Albanian border authorities three times. During the third contact the president of the local joint commission personally came out, Gzim Goci was his name, who told me that all Albanians can cross into Albanian territory without any documents at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could just -- if we could just focus on this for a moment. The president of the joint local commission, Gzim Goci, which country's authorities did he represent?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the local joint commission on the Albanian side. I think that he had the rank of a general. I'm not sure, but I think that that was his rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would that local joint commission on the Albanian side be an organ of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or of the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It was an organ of the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this local joint commission, is that a body that functions at all of the border crossings of Federal Yugoslavia with other internationally recognised countries?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: The local joint commission was tasked with resolving border incidents on the entire territory, meaning that all the sectors had a local joint commission on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And backing up a bit, you talked about the phone calls you had with the administration of the border police in Belgrade. Do you recall the office that you called or the person that you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I called the chief of the section because this was not an ordinary event. I called the chief of the police department at the administration, told him, and I got his permission that if the Albanian border authorities were willing to receive these people, they should be allowed to leave after their particulars were taken, and this meant even taking a thumb -- an index finger-print from of-age persons. Since the majority of these people were women and children, I only took the finger-prints of some four or five men.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're at the 5.15 point. I believe that's the point that the break is scheduled under the new -- under the revised sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, can you tell us when the mines along the road to the Zur intersection were laid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the date, but I know when there was a danger of land NATO forces coming or crossing into the SR -- the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We need a break now. Could you, while we have the break, please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you again at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we left off talking about this group of 90-plus persons that came to the Vrbnica border crossing on the 27th of March, 1999. Can I ask you to look at 6D1497, a document from the Vrbnica border station. And once that comes up, sir, I'll ask you to take a look at this and let me know if indeed this incident that is being described here is, in fact, the incident that you have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the official note number 72, dated the 27th of March, 1999. There is another official note on account of this particular incident, and you can see here what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to these persons, this group, you indicated there were four men whose finger-prints you took. Was it the four men -- strike that. Did you know any of these persons personally prior to the incident?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was born in Prizren. Everybody knows me there. I even socialised with some of them in the field of sports, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you talked about how you had tried to persuade them to go back to their homes. Did they have occasion to tell you why they were leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Several times I tried to dissuade them, I even beseeched them to go back to their homes, but they were so persistent, I simply had to relent. It was children, women, and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could please enlighten us. What was the reason that they gave for having to leave their homes? What were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They gave several reasons. They said that it was due to NATO bombing, because of the danger, that there were positions of the Army of Yugoslavia near their village, and then since they were afraid of NATO bombing, there they were afraid and they felt that they would be safer in Albania. That's what they stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said that they did not have passports. Was it the custom -- was it the regular procedure or was it the regular expectancy to have women and children to have their own separate passports among the Kosovo Albanian ethnic minority in Kosovo-Metohija in the time-period prior to this occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Invariably -- actually, could you please repeat your question. I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and rephrase the question. I'm told the translation wasn't -- let me try and simplify the question. Did you expect the women and children to have passports of their own right and accord, given your knowledge and experience of the area and the experiences you've had up until that point working at -- working in the position that you were working?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Not only while working in this position. These people are my neighbours. I was born in Kosovo and Metohija, and I know that the Albanian ethnic minority as of late, that is to say after 1990, they started ignoring our state organs, they did not get personal IDs, and there are some people who actually never got a personal ID any time in their life, let alone another document. They refused everything that had to do with the state. So this was a singular case. We never had a case like that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at line 4, page 58, they did not get personal IDs, I believe in Serbian they did not ask nor get personal IDs. Mr. Ognjenovic, is that correct? Is my intervention correct in terms of what you said in response to my question?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they themselves did not ask for these documents, and hence they did not get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these men, some of them you say you personally knew, did they give you any reason why they did not have valid passports on them when they came to the border crossing or identification cards?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: When they arrived and when they made their statement, they stated that their personal IDs were kept at the Prizren SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after you let these persons pass, did you take any steps to investigate that particular claim, that the personal ID -- personal ID cards were retained at the Prizren SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I called the duty service at the Prizren SUP, and I was told that no documents had been detained or retained or handed over to the duty service of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe you had already identified that the reason for letting these persons cross the border was humanitarian in nature. Had there ever been similar situations previously to your knowledge on the territory of the former SFRY where, for humanitarian reasons, the rules were of such to permit persons to cross?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The example of the refugees from Bosnia, Croatia, Romania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have just a question. What was the use of the ID cards, identity cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The citizens were required to have identification cards. Now, you are telling us that these people did not go for identification cards and their story about having left them at -- at that place with the SUP was not accepted. Now, how did they carry on then their day-to-day business without the cards? I mean, that is why I have asked that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that everyone did not go out to obtain a card. Only individuals did not. When they really needed something, then they would get these documents; otherwise, women in particular almost never went to get personal IDs, whereas men who went out to work did have identity cards and passports. Women, very few, especially in the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in answer to one of my previous questions you already confirmed that you never received any orders of any kind to take ID cards, travel documents, or car registration plates. Did, in fact, this situation occur, did the police take such items from persons at the Vrbnica border crossing in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the border crossing every day. I did not notice and I did not see -- had I noticed, I certainly would have taken measures against that policeman, I mean a policeman who would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as a practical matter, do you believe you had the manpower to accomplish such a task, given the number of persons that were crossing the border on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly didn't have enough people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you spoke with the persons of Albanian ethnicity at the border, was this in Serbian or in their own language?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It was in their language. I speak excellent Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of persons of other national or ethnic groups that were leaving their homes in addition to Albanians within the Prizren area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I do have such knowledge, and I saw members of the Turkish national minority going to Turkey and Serbs were going to Serbia, my own family included. I had to evacuate them from the house where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when and why did you evacuate your own family from the familial home where you were born?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I lived in the country, in the vicinity of my village there were quite a few members of the KLA. In my village there were 10.000 Albanians and only about 20 Serbs. Because of possible clashes between members of the KLA and our security organs, I was compelled to evacuate my family, I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know the fate of some of your ethnic Albanian friends and neighbours in this regard, did they leave; and if so, do you know reasons for which they left their homes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have quite a few examples of my neighbours who left their homes, against their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some concrete examples of some of your friends and neighbours of ethnic Albanian background and the circumstances regarding their departure from their homes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I can. I know the names, but for the sake of their own safety and security I don't know if I should give their names because they are still in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the safety of the third parties that still live in Kosovo whom the witness has knowledge of, I would ask that we go into closed session to deal with that part of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Private session will be enough for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us of any specific acts undertaken by the Serbian police at the Vrbnica border crossing station to help and assist persons of ethnic Albanian ethnicity during 1999, and specifically during the time-period of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We helped the sickly and frail. We gave them the little food we had for ourselves, that is to say the packed lunches that we had. Since the weather was warm, there was water running 24 hours a day so that they could wash up, freshen themselves, and so on. I have an example, when the village of Korisa was bombed, a husband and a wife from the area of Djakovica who had been wounded came there and they wanted to cross over to Albania, and I said that I should call an ambulance so that we provide medical assistance to them. They said that they didn't want to because they said that at the Albanian border crossing there was an ambulance waiting for them, that they had already agreed upon all of that with people from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for purposes of clarification, you say when the village of Korisa was bombed. What was your information about who undertook that act of bombing?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was, but I believe that it was the NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any incidents at the Vrbnica border crossing where persons died or suffered serious injury?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I remember very well. I remember a family from the outskirts of Pristina who had a Lada type vehicle, and they disregarded the instructions that the policemen gave them not to take the left lane and they came across a land-mine and five members of his family got killed in that car. Three days later I called the same person to cross the border and to collect his wife's body that was in the chapel in Prizren. He came to see me at my office and he said, I cannot go to Prizren. Let them bury her wherever they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take this one step at a time. At page 65, line 2 of the transcript you are recorded as saying: "Three days later you called the same person to cross the border ..." Is that, in fact, what you said?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because he was already in Kukes. That is the first inhabited town on the other side of the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of this individual and any of his family members who perished when he drove across the mine?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I had an official note compiled about that. I know Ibish was his name and he was from the village of Vragolije from the area surrounding Pristina. I don't remember any other details. I know that his wife got killed, his mother, his son, and his daughter, as far as I can remember. He's the only one who survived unharmed and another child was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can ask you, was, in fact, the border crossing mined before the commencement of the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- a leading question -- well, it's too late to object that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question was asked earlier by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought so as well, but I don't recall the answer off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the answer, Mr. Ognjenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't mined before the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hardly leading in the circumstances, Mr. Stamp. But it's a different answer from the one that was given earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I said, I don't have in front of me the ability to scroll the transcript, but in any event I can perhaps get back to that if I feel that it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to receive any notifications or announcements from the MUP staff in Pristina during 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The previous answer is on page 55 at line 19 -- sorry, line 20 when the witness said: "I don't remember the date, but I know when there was a danger of land NATO forces coming or crossing into the FRY." Now, that's a very broad answer, but I took it as being at the time that they were first aware of that; obviously, that was the wrong inference to draw from the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can -- I forget if I asked this before. Did you have occasion -- prior to the NATO bombings, did you have occasion to interact at all with members of the OSCE-KVM mission; and if so, could you describe those contacts for us?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Representatives of the OSCE came on only one occasion to my border crossing, they came to my office, we talked, they stayed for about half an hour, and then they returned to -- in the direction of Prizren. They wanted to know about the situation in the neighbouring villages which were along the borderline, and I told them that that was not under my jurisdiction, I was not informed about that, that they should go to the SUP in Prizren and ask them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you familiar with an individual by the name of Hysni Kryeziu, K-r-y-e-z-i-u?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: It's my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. -- do you know a Haki Cuni who would have been 65 years of age in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How do you know that individual?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: He was also my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything you know about the circumstances surrounding the 1999 death of Haki Cuni for whom Hysni Kryeziu testified here that the same was killed by the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Haki Cuni from the village of Dusanovo is still alive and living in his village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I found out from a friend who came to Belgrade about a month ago and he told me about this person, that he was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to identify this person? First of all, was he -- this person who told you about this, was he an ethnic Albanian and where is he from?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Dusanovo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could counsel assist us by pointing out the -- by citing where the evidence is from Hysni Kryeziu in respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure, that's the 92 ter statement of Hysni Kryeziu, P2514. And this particular incident in the -- and this particular incident is on page 2. One moment. Pardon me, page 3, paragraph 3, on that page about the Haki Cuni killing. In e-court it's page 9 in the English the third paragraph -- the second full paragraph, but the third breaking on that page since that OTP statement did not have paragraph numbers I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the individual from your village who told you about the fact that Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A matter for the record, the name spelled in the statement as indicated by my friend is spelled C with a -- C-u-n-i with an accent on the C and it really reads that: "Haki Cuni, 65-years-old, was taken out of his house into a van. I saw him taken away on the police van and I later learned that he had been killed. I don't know any other details about this incident or the reason why they took him." So I don't think what my friend said about the witness Kreyziu said is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly something you can cross-examine on and it's something you can in due course also address us on. So please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we still haven't discussed this matter, sir. The individual from your home individual, the ethnic Albanian who came to Belgrade and who confirmed that Mr. Cuni is still alive, would you be able to give us that individual's name?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, we should go into private session for the name of this -- of this person for purposes of safety of third persons not before this Chamber who still reside in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there some reason why he should be at risk? There's been a clear indication of a reason in each case so far, but in this one is there a reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, is there any reason why you would not want to identify this individual in open court?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the person could have problems where he lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in light of the turbulent situation down on the ground in Kosovo and Metohija according to the news reports, I would rather err on the side of the caution, especially where the safety of an individual is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I generally would agree with you, but at the moment I really don't see what the point in issue is in this instance. Is this not an Albanian living in Albania who on the face of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Albanian living in Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, in Kosovo, yes, but who on the face of it has no reason to fear repercussions for simply claiming that someone is actually alive? There's -- we -- there's no point in us wasting time on this. Let's go into private session, but generally speaking we are resistant to that unless there's a reason for it. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Prosecution witnesses had us go into private session to discuss the names of persons who actually came and testified later to say the matters that they said were not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we hope we've learned from that experience, Mr. Ivetic, and it would be a sad Trial Chamber that didn't try to improve as the trial progressed; however, we will grant your wish on this occasion with reservation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did there come to be a time at the Vrbnica border post crossing and police station when ethnic Albanians or any persons, actually, crossing the border would discard documents, personal documents; and if so, could you tell us the circumstances behind the same?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to the actual border crossing area, since the column was about some 20 kilometres away from the border crossing, they probably communicated amongst themselves, and whoever came to the border crossing, whatever documents they had with them, they would throw them away. Some people had IDs, some had passports. Some kept their passports, but the ID cards were discarded by everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the column was very long, sometimes people would wait even for ten days to be able to cross. They were tired, they were hungry. We didn't have the option of trying to dissuade them from leaving. A couple of times we even lowered the ramp, but this is not something that can be described, it's only something that a person has to live through. They all had the desire to leave the territory of Serbia. They would state different reasons, mostly the NATO bombing and the conflicts between the KLA and members of our army, although there were other reasons too. Some of them said that they had relatives there and it would be easier for them to receive political asylum without documents in one of the western countries. That is also one of the reasons they would give.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back just a little bit. The interpreters could not hear one of your answers. I will -- it's impossible to ask you to repeat the whole thing. Let me try and direct your attention to it, and because I believe there's also an error in the transcript at line 22. Was it ID cards or passports that were being discarded by these persons as they crossed the region of the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: ID cards and passports by individuals. Most of the passports were red passports which had expired. They just wanted to show others around them that they had hated the Republic of Serbia and they would throw them away. We just watched this without saying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think the -- at line 19 the "by individuals" relates to the passports, but we can have CLSS verify that translation. Do you have any idea of the percentage of those crossing the border who discarded their documents, their ID cards in this manner -- pardon me. Strike that. Do you have any idea of the percentage of those crossing the border who discarded their passports in this manner, the red expired SFRY passports?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the percentage, but about 1 per cent of those who left were persons of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't sound correct, Mr. Ivetic. Let's go back a little. What documents were being discarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the documents that were issued by the SUP, all the documents by the Serb organs were discarded, driver's licences, traffic licences, personal IDs, passports, and even licence plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The overall result of the answers you've given so far indicates that there were some documents that people were inclined to retain. Did you mention any documents that people were inclined to retain rather than discard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What documents were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Passports, travel papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You also mentioned the discarding of certain passports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which passports were they -- were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were our red passports with "SFRY" on the cover. These were replaced by new blue passports. So these red ones were discarded, the ones that had already expired. This was not something that happened in each case, but it was something that we did observe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over to you, Mr. Ivetic. If you want to check percentages, it's a matter for you. That's too complicated for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the ID cards that would be discarded, what did -- that were being discarded, what did the employees of the border crossing at Vrbnica do with respect to the same?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: We collected all the documents and placed them in a room, driver's licences, car papers were something that we gave to the Prizren SUP, the traffic police stations. Licence plates found in the border crossing area were returned to the SUP Prizren, the vehicle registration department. Since there was a large number of personal ID cards, we were unable to sort them by place of issue. They remained in a room at the building at the border post. Perhaps there was a full bag or sack of these left behind after we had left the border post building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The documents that were returned to the SUPs, was that in accordance with standing law on such documents when found or discarded?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the red SFRY passports that you had described, were these passports valid for exit of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They were not valid for exit because new passports had been issued, but if they were still valid the persons could return to the country from abroad, they could come back to their country. But they could not use them to leave the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the border police station at Vrbnica undertake to do physical searches of the persons who were crossing the border in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not because there was no theoretical chance of doing that. There were many people there. I mentioned that the column was 20 kilometres long, women, children, tractors, buses, trucks, there was no time for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple questions with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Ognjenovic, I'm Djuro Cepic and I represent the Defence of General Lazarevic. I just have a few questions for you. You mentioned two check-points, one mixed check-point near the village of Zur and the other one at the exit from Prizren that was just a check-point of the Army of Yugoslavia. I'm interested in the one by Prizren. You said that you often travelled from Vrbnica to Prizren. Were you ever stopped at that check-point?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you tell me about this road from the Vrbnica border crossing to the town of Prizren. You said that its length is -- that 6 kilometres of that road had been mined. I would be interested in the following. As you moved along, did you perhaps see soldiers of the VJ warning civilians not to go off that road because there were mines there? We heard General Bozidar Delic testifying about that here. I don't know if you have any personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I saw policemen, I mean soldiers, but I did not hear what it was that they were saying. But I did see them every time I went by. Now, what it was that they were saying, I didn't hear that so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned this bridge at the very border. You mentioned the mining and the obstacles. Do you know that half of that bridge is actually on our side of the border?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know. The borderline is halfway along the bridge, there's a red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question, Mr. Ognjenovic. You mentioned the reasons why people were leaving Kosovo and you pointed out that to the best of your knowledge one of the reasons was that there was a danger of NATO bombing the positions of the Army of Yugoslavia that were near the villages which would jeopardize the population. My question: Did anyone tell you maybe that members of the Army of Yugoslavia had forced them out of their homes?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No one said that to me and they probably would have told me because everybody knows me. They certainly would have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ognjenovic. No questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ognjenovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, this column that was 20 kilometres long, when are you speaking about? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the date?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but from the 24th when the first group left up until the 10th of June. Sometimes there was a 5- or 10-kilometre long column, sometimes even 20 kilometres long. It depends. Albanian border organs were there. There would be a bottleneck there in the traffic, people simply couldn't get through and that is why there was a long column.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to know if the evidence you gave about people throwing away their documents and car licences and so, was this something that occurred on one day with this column of 20 kilometres or was it something that occurred on more than one day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: That occurred several times, but I am not claiming that everyone discarded them. Most of them said that they don't have them, that somebody kept their documents, that they forgot them at home. That is why I said 1 to 2 per cent of the total number, so I'm trying to say it's not everybody. They came up with all sorts of excuses for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So people -- or let me ask you this: Approximately how many people went through your border crossing to Albania during the period of the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: According to my records, about 430.000 persons. The record day was the 29th of March, 100.000 in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the -- you saw them disposing of their ID cards, this 2 per cent that you speak of, you actually witnessed this?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I did see that, but we found these ID cards. It's not that we were standing there when they were passing. I mean, it wasn't a regular border crossing. This was extraordinary traffic of passengers. It was not regular traffic, and there wasn't document control or any other kind of control, any other kind of checks. It was impossible. Children, women, full tractors, it was impossible to check everyone. There weren't regular checks. They threw this away and they would pass by. Nobody checked them. From the 25th of March onwards -- I mean, the 27th of March, that's when the first group came, and no one checked anyone anymore. We were not checking these persons who were leaving the territory of Serbia on their own at the Vrbnica border crossing. No one checked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what became of those documents that the people threw away?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that's been asked and answered. I think he went into some detail with that in the direct, unless there's a specific type of document that we didn't cover. I thought we covered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, what's to prevent cross-examination on something you've covered? Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What became of those documents you collected?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said, everything that we collected in the area of the border crossing, the driver's licences and the traffic -- to Prizren and then the licence plates to the automobile association in Prizren. The personal IDs remained in one room at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you leave them there? Did you leave the personal IDs there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: After we withdrew, these personal IDs remained in that room. I assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were these personal IDs government property?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: These personal IDs are issued by the secretariat of the interior at the place of residence of the said persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were they government property?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: They are just issued by the state. This is a personal document of each and every individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you keep a record of how many ID cards you collected there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not technically possible to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you picked them up, put them in a bag, and put them in a room. And am I to understand that after you did that you never had opportunity to check and make a record of those IDs that you collected?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that there was a sack full. We tried to categorize them by the secretariats that had issued them at first, but afterwards it became impossible. We just left it there, and when we withdrew from the station that stayed behind in that room. As for the driver's licences and the traffic licences, there were less of those, and we collected them and returned them to the authority that had issued them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That included the licence plates on motor vehicles. You picked up those as well and returned them. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We returned that too to the secretariat of the interior in Prizren, to the department for registration, the automobile association, that is where all the licence plates were left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So did -- the vehicles that passed through without licence plates, that passed through your border post without licence plates, did you see the occupants of these vehicles, did you actually witness them taking off their licence plates and throwing them away?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Then as a police officer it didn't occur to you that maybe these vehicles were, therefore, stolen?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: There were such cases as well when that was our suspicion, that there were stolen vehicles. We would confiscate such vehicles with a proper document. If a vehicle would come with a broken door or a broken window, then we would keep such vehicles. We confiscated five such vehicles and handed them over to the secretariat of the interior in Prizren when there were suspicions that this was the result of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but didn't you find it suspicious that somebody should be driving a motor vehicle in columns across the border out of the country and wanted to throw away the documents that identify the motor vehicle? Didn't that raise your suspicions about these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: When I saw people taking off their licence plates, I would make them put them back where they belonged, and there are others who I did not see during the night. I mean, nobody could see them. They would just throw away these licence plates. When we would see this happen, then we would warn these people and then these people would return the licence plates onto their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Why I was asking you these questions is that you've told us earlier that you just watched them doing it and did nothing; now you are saying that you did something, you told them to put it back?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA OGNJENOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that those people who I saw doing that, I told them to return it. As for those who I did not see, they discarded their licence plates and they went by. I didn't see them. I mean, there weren't regular checks anymore at the exit point from the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, can you find a suitable opportunity to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ognjenovic, we have to terminate our sitting for today and resume tomorrow. That means that you will require to return to complete your evidence tomorrow; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom. Meanwhile, it is essential that you have no communication whatsoever with anyone, anyone at all, about the evidence in this case. You can talk about any other subject, but absolutely off limits for any communication is any aspect of the evidence in this case. Now would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
